## Visual audit: VX01

**Directly visible observations.** Image 1 shows a densely occupied, aged wooden workbench against vertical wood paneling. Image 2 reproduces the broad arrangement: a bench with several open drawers, a central foreground seat, tools and containers on the worktop, a raised circular fixture, a wall shelf, and portions of furniture at the sides. Image 3 appears visually identical to Image 2 at the supplied resolution; no visible change between those two renders can be established.

The reference has substantially denser small-object coverage: numerous distinct metal hand tools, handled implements, containers and drawer contents are visible across the worktop and in several drawers. The render suggests tool groups and a row of handled implements, but many forms are simplified, and the drawers look comparatively empty or dark. Occlusion and the small image size prevent a reliable count of objects, particularly inside drawers. The reference’s raised circular fixture has multiple visible levels and radial compartments; the render shows a simpler single tray on a stem. The right-hand tool rack and adjacent stacked items are represented schematically.

In Image 1, the drawers, tabletop and foreground seat show mottling, scratches, stains, grain and irregular wear; metal surfaces vary in color and reflectivity. Image 2 has lighter, more uniform wood and a pale worktop and seat, with much less visible surface variation. Its small tools are also less clearly differentiated from the work surface. The render is visibly grainy, especially in shadowed areas.

The reference’s tools lie in close visual proximity across the tabletop, with drawer fronts staggered beneath it and the seat centered in front. The render retains these broad adjacencies and open-drawer poses, although the drawer arrangement and apparent contents differ. Image 1 also includes a more prominent left-side bench and right-edge dark structure. In Image 2, the left extension and a narrow dark diagonal element on the right provide partial counterparts. These projected adjacencies do not prove physical contact.

Both views look downward toward the bench from the front. The rendered view is more front-on and orderly, while the reference shows a stronger sense of depth and a more crowded, irregular arrangement. Image 1 has warmer, directional lighting, stronger contrast and detailed highlights; Image 2 is more evenly lit and pastel, with softer material definition. Differences in perspective, shadow and rendering can obscure or change the apparent shapes of small parts.

**Geometric hypotheses, not established facts.** The reference fixture may consist of stacked divided trays, whereas the rendered fixture may have only one modeled tray; the images do not establish hidden geometry. Some rendered tools may be separate simplified objects or texture-like representations, but their construction and actual contact with the bench cannot be determined from pixels. No teacher diagnosis, student adoption or causal improvement is inferable from these images. This deterministic small sample does not support conclusions about all Scene RSI experiments.

**Sources:** Image 1: `/srv/lab-disks/disk2/users/xymo/Documents/Codex/2026-11-02/scene-rsi-rsi-1-3d-blender/outputs/scene_rsi_v2/results/r1/fixed_h0/H0/development/commons_129095630/reference.png`; Image 2: `/srv/lab-disks/disk2/users/xymo/Documents/Codex/2026-11-02/scene-rsi-rsi-1-3d-blender/outputs/scene_rsi_v2/results/r1/fixed_h0/H0/development/commons_129095630/steps/002/final.png`; Image 3: `/srv/lab-disks/disk2/users/xymo/Documents/Codex/2026-11-02/scene-rsi-rsi-1-3d-blender/outputs/scene_rsi_v2/results/r1/fixed_h0/H0/development/commons_129095630/final.png`.

## Visual audit — VX02

**Sources:** Image 1, reference: `/srv/lab-disks/disk2/users/xymo/Documents/Codex/2026-11-02/scene-rsi-rsi-1-3d-blender/outputs/scene_rsi_v2_1/results/r1/fixed_h0/H0/development/commons_187101683/reference.png`; Image 2, first available rendered step: `/srv/lab-disks/disk2/users/xymo/Documents/Codex/2026-11-02/scene-rsi-rsi-1-3d-blender/outputs/scene_rsi_v2_1/results/r1/fixed_h0/H0/development/commons_187101683/steps/002/final.png`; Image 3, final selected render: `/srv/lab-disks/disk2/users/xymo/Documents/Codex/2026-11-02/scene-rsi-rsi-1-3d-blender/outputs/scene_rsi_v2_1/results/r1/fixed_h0/H0/development/commons_187101683/final.png`.

### Directly visible observations

- **Coverage and arrangement:** Images 2 and 3 retain the reference’s main composition: a warm-colored sofa behind a dark coffee table, two white cups with saucers and flat rectangular items, a central potted flowering plant, and a curtain at right. They also show two sofa pillows. The plant, cups, and table overlap in a broadly similar front-to-back arrangement to Image 1, although the rendered sofa fills more of the frame and the table is more heavily cropped.
- **Visible parts and pose:** In Image 1 the sofa has rounded, irregular upholstery, visible cushion separations, broad arms, and a textured lower front. In Images 2 and 3 its cushions and arms are smoother, squarer and more uniformly defined. The left pillow is more upright and rectangular in the renders; the right pillow is also more distinctly outlined. The two cups flank the plant in all three images, but their apparent positions and handle orientations differ. Overlap and occlusion prevent confirmation of physical contact or hidden parts.
- **Materials and detail:** The reference sofa has mottled, velvety-looking shading and creases; the rendered sofa has a more even, peach-colored surface. The reference table shows subtle surface variation, while the rendered table is flatter and uniformly dark. The plant in the renders reproduces green foliage and pale blue flower clusters, though the flowers and leaves appear simplified and less naturalistic. The reference curtain has broad, soft folds and reflective highlights; the rendered curtain has narrower, more regular vertical folds.
- **Camera and lighting:** Image 1 shows more of the sofa’s front and table legs, with stronger depth perspective and a darker foreground. Images 2 and 3 have a more frontal, elevated-looking view of the sofa and tabletop; the table extends beyond the right and lower image boundaries. The reference has directional light, pronounced shadow and shallow-looking background softness. The renders are brighter and more evenly lit, with conspicuous grain and less nuanced shading.
- **First and final:** Images 2 and 3 appear identical at the supplied resolution. The visible evidence therefore does not establish a change between these two supplied renders; it does not rule out unshown attempts or changes.

### Geometric hypotheses and limits

The differing framing could reflect camera placement, focal length, object proportions, or a combination; the images alone do not identify which. Apparent gaps or overlaps around cushions, cups, saucers and the pot do not prove whether surfaces touch. Occlusion and render noise also limit assessment of small details and hidden object count. This deterministic small sample is not a conclusion about all Scene RSI experiments, nor does it establish diagnosis, adoption, or causal improvement.

## Limited visual audit: VX03

**Sources:** Image 1, reference: `/srv/lab-disks/disk2/users/xymo/Documents/Codex/2026-11-02/scene-rsi-rsi-1-3d-blender/outputs/scene_rsi_v2_2/results/r1/fixed_h/H0/fixed_version_test/commons_31294395/reference.png`; Image 2, first available rendered step: `.../commons_31294395/steps/002/final.png`; Image 3, selected final: `.../commons_31294395/final.png`. The ellipses abbreviate the same directory prefix as Image 1. Images 2 and 3 appear visually identical at the supplied resolution, so no visible change between them can be established.

### Directly visible observations

- **Coverage and arrangement:** The renders include the major visible categories: two windows, a dark bed with pale bedding, an olive armchair, a blue-and-gold folding screen, small furniture, wall pictures and rugs (Images 1–3). Their arrangement is approximate rather than exact. The reference bed and chair dominate the foreground; the rendered furniture appears smaller within a wider view. The reference includes a door behind the screen and a chair beside the bed; neither is clearly distinguishable in the renders. Occlusion and simplification limit conclusions about what is actually present.
- **Materials and detail:** The reference has densely patterned wallpaper, detailed dark wood, creased bedding, upholstery texture and patterned rugs. The renders use mostly flat beige walls and simplified surfaces; the screen retains conspicuous blue and gold shapes, but its figurative detail is reduced. The rendered bed and pillows have fewer visible folds, and the chair lacks the reference’s visibly tufted back.
- **Visible adjacency and pose:** In Image 1, the chair overlaps the bed’s near end in projection, while the screen rises behind them. In Images 2–3, a gap is visible between much of the chair and bed, and the screen is partly obscured by the chair. The reference chair is angled with its back and side prominent; the rendered chair faces more toward the camera. The bed’s orientation is broadly similar, though its proportions and placement differ in projection. These overlaps and gaps alone do not establish physical contact or separation in three dimensions.
- **Camera and lighting:** Image 1 has a closer, more immersive view, strong window brightness and darker foreground furniture. Images 2–3 show more floor and room boundaries, including a large dark-gray region above the room, and have more even illumination. The renders are visibly grainy, softening fine edges and materials; the bright reference windows also obscure exterior detail.

### Geometric hypotheses and limits

The wider-looking rendered composition may reflect a more distant camera, a different field of view, different object scale, or a combination. The altered chair–bed overlap may likewise reflect placement, camera angle or both. The images alone cannot resolve these alternatives or establish hidden object counts.

This is one deterministically sampled case, not evidence about all Scene RSI experiments. The images do not establish a teacher diagnosis, student adoption, or a causal improvement.

## Limited visual audit — VX04

**Sources.** The images are cited below using this common directory:
`/srv/lab-disks/disk2/users/xymo/Documents/Codex/2026-11-02/scene-rsi-rsi-1-3d-blender/outputs/scene_rsi_v3/preparation/second_smoke/historical_r1_C2_start/development/commons_109923183/1/`
- Image 1, reference: `reference.png`
- Image 2, first available rendered step: `steps/001/final.png`
- Image 3, final selected render: `final.png`

### Directly visible observations

- **Coverage and pose:** Image 1 shows a chaise longue with a raised, curved back at left, a long upholstered seat, exposed ornamental frame and legs, and a pillow. Paneled walls, a dark wood floor, curtains, and part of another chair are also visible. Images 2 and 3 depict the same broad arrangement: a left-raised chaise, pillow-like form, paneled wall, floor, and a small cropped foreground object at left. The renders omit or crop much of the curtain and other chair. A small dark green rectangular item is visible on the seat in all three images.
- **Shape and adjacency:** In image 1, the back sweeps into a relatively tall side arm, whose frame visually meets the seat rail; the seat has a rounded far end. The renders have a more segmented-looking back and a straighter, slab-like seat. Image 3 shows a prominent curved side rail alongside the back and a long rail below the seat; their visible junctions are simpler than the reference’s carved transitions. Image 2’s frame and legs are smaller and less distinct at its wider framing. Overlap and occlusion prevent confirmation of physical contact between parts.
- **Materials and detail:** Image 1 has pale patterned upholstery, a textured cream pillow, aged green-gray wood with decorative carving, and dark, reflective-looking flooring. The renders retain light upholstery, fine seat stripes and a muted frame, but the upholstery pattern, carved ornament and pillow texture are much less apparent. Their floors appear as broad, regularly separated boards, lighter in image 2 and darker in image 3. The wall moldings are recognizable but more regular and simplified than in the reference.
- **View and lighting:** Image 1 is viewed obliquely from above, with the chaise filling much of the frame and its near side and rounded end visible. Image 2 places a smaller chaise farther back in a wider view. Image 3 brings it closer and larger, with a more nearly side-on impression and a more rectangular-looking seat. Both renders are grainy and bright; image 2 is especially washed out. Image 3 has stronger floor contrast but still loses fine detail in the pale surfaces.

### Geometric hypotheses and limits

The renders’ back, arm and seat may use simpler underlying forms than the reference, and the image 3 seat may be less tapered or rounded. Those are hypotheses from projected outlines: perspective, lighting, occlusion and render noise also affect the comparison. The visible images do not establish hidden object counts or physical contact, nor do they establish a teacher diagnosis, student adoption, or a causal improvement between images 2 and 3. This deterministic small sample is not a conclusion about all Scene RSI experiments.

## Limited visual audit — VX05, scene_rsi_v3, bw_0017

### Directly visible observations

**Coverage and detail.** The reference (image 1) shows an industrial hall with several large silver processing units, raised platforms, yellow guardrails and staircases, a green vertical tank, and extensive foreground conveyor equipment. The first render (image 2) includes the hall structure, tank, yellow stairs and rails, and blue conveyor-like foreground surfaces, but its roof and elevated viewpoint obscure much of the machinery area. The final render (image 3) makes the raised machinery and walkway more visible: two light-colored machine masses and duct-like arches are discernible. It still represents fewer small components and less of the dense foreground equipment visible in the reference. Occlusion and image resolution limit any count of parts.

The reference has varied metallic reflections, detailed rails, rollers, pipes and machine faces. Both renders use simpler surfaces and repeated linear elements. In image 3, the dark slatted machine face and blue foreground strips provide recognizable detail, but fine components and material variation remain less distinct. Visible grain in both renders further limits assessment.

**Adjacency and pose.** In image 1, stairs rise toward the guarded elevated machinery area; the green tank appears in front of it, with conveyors occupying the lower foreground. Images 2 and 3 retain a similar broad arrangement of tank, elevated yellow-railed area, stairs and foreground conveyors. In image 3, a staircase crosses visually in front of the tank area, and a tall stairway stands at the right end of the platform. These are screen-space relationships: the images alone do not establish physical contact or exact depth alignment.

**Camera and lighting.** Image 1 uses an interior, roughly eye-level oblique view, with the machinery prominent across the middle and bright directional highlights. Image 2 looks down from outside or above the hall boundary, so the broad roof dominates the upper image and hides the principal machinery. Image 3 moves to an interior, more frontal view, closer to the reference’s presentation, although its foreground conveyor is cropped and the composition and perspective remain different. Both renders are visibly noisy; image 2 also has a conspicuously bright roof patch, while image 3 has dark overhead areas and unevenly bright machinery. These rendering effects obscure some detail.

### Geometric hypotheses and limits

The railings, stairs and supports in the renders suggest an elevated platform, and the curved forms above the machines suggest ducts. Their precise geometry, connections and hidden components cannot be verified from these views. The final view reveals more machinery than the first available view, but the images do not establish why the views differ or demonstrate a causal improvement, teacher diagnosis or student adoption.

## Limited visual audit — VX06, scene_rsi_v3, bw_0031

**Directly visible observations.** Image 1 is a poster-like reference combining title text, a yellow electrical schematic panel and a historical photograph of a control room. The photograph contains a long, angled control console, rows of individually outlined instruments and switches, tall rear cabinets, a doorway or dark vertical recess, and a separate console at right. Images 2 and 3 show a simplified, mostly pale enclosure with a floor, roof and right side, a central sloped console, and a narrow instrument strip behind it. They appear visually identical at the supplied resolution; no visible change between the first available step and final selection can be established.

The render covers the broad idea of a control-room console but not the reference poster’s text, yellow diagram or graphic layout. Within the room view, the main console has many small marks suggesting controls, but they are less distinct than the reference’s outlined meters, switches and panel divisions. The separate right-hand console and much of the rear cabinet detail are not clearly visible. Occlusion and the render’s brightness limit any inference about what might exist outside or behind visible surfaces.

The reference photograph has varied dark and light surfaces, visible panel seams, instrument borders and a textured floor. The render uses largely uniform light-gray or white surfaces; fine controls are faint, and grain and bright highlights further reduce detail. Its roof has a bright rectangular patch, and a small bright mark appears on the right wall. The reference photograph is comparatively evenly exposed, although its printed, aged appearance also softens detail.

In the reference photograph, the long console runs diagonally across the foreground, with the instrument wall immediately behind it in the image. In the render, the sloped console sits visually in front of the rear strip and above a block-like base; the roof and right wall frame and partly obscure the interior. These are image-plane adjacencies, not proof of physical contact.

The reference photograph looks into the room from an elevated oblique viewpoint, with the console dominating the lower foreground. The render takes a more exterior, elevated view of an open-fronted box: the broad roof and right side occupy much of the frame, while the console appears smaller. The poster’s separate diagram is front-facing rather than part of that room perspective.

**Geometric hypotheses, not established facts.** The rendered roof and right wall may be modeled as enclosing geometry, and the console may be a separate sloped panel on a base. The bright roof patch may be a light or an illuminated opening. The image alone cannot establish those constructions, physical contacts, or hidden object counts.

**Sources and scope.** Image 1: `/srv/lab-disks/disk2/users/xymo/Documents/Codex/2026-11-02/scene-rsi-rsi-1-3d-blender/outputs/scene_rsi_v3/results/H01/selection/bw_0031/1/reference.png`.
